Be a Hero for Your Heroes

  • November 10, 2026
  • Nicole Nash
  • Photo Credit: ATA

Share:  

Finding connection, purpose and a place to belong through archery.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:54
Instaread

When military service ends, coming home isn’t always an easy transition. For many veterans, leaving the military and returning to civilian life means leaving behind the people, daily routines and sense of purpose they knew for years. One day, they’re part of a team with a shared mission. Then that chapter is over. The question becomes: Where do I belong now?

For veterans who attended the 2026 HHA USA Centershot Blue Mission 43 and the 2026 Centershot Blue Outpost in Green Bay, Wisconsin, archery helped answer this question.

They come from diverse backgrounds and branches of service. Some return to a childhood love of archery, while others pick up a bow for the first time. What they share is a desire to reconnect, build friendships and restore the feeling of belonging to a team.

That sense of belonging can take many forms: time on an archery range, a few arrows in the backyard or basement, or a day in the woods bowhunting. Whether enjoying the quiet of the woods or sharing a hunt with a friend, archery gives them a chance to reconnect with something they love.

Shooting a bow takes focus and concentration. From setting your stance and hooking up to the D-loop to drawing the bow, finding your anchor point, aiming and releasing the arrow with proper follow-through, each step asks you to be present. As your attention and focus shift to the shot, everything gets a little quieter. One veteran shared, “While I am shooting my bow, the demons in my head become quieter.” That’s why he makes time for archery every day, even if it’s just a few arrows at home.

That quiet matters. So does the company.

Time on the range brings people together. Veterans share stories, build friendships and spend time with others who understand their experiences. Several talked about how hard it was to find that sense of community after leaving the military. Now, many share their experiences and reach out to help other veterans.

The impact doesn’t stop with those who attend. Some veterans returned to Centershot Blue events as volunteers after participating first. They know what a welcoming community can mean, and they’re helping make that possible for others.

As a civilian, I may never fully understand what these veterans have experienced or what they carry with them. But listening to their stories left me thinking about what happens after we say, “Thank you for your service.”

Gratitude matters. But so does showing up.

This Veterans Day, be a hero for your heroes. Reach out to a veteran you know. Don’t wait for a special occasion or the perfect words. Pick up the phone. Say hello. Invite them to spend an afternoon shooting together.

Sometimes, the best way to say thank you is to remind someone they still belong.
